In Retail & Consumer Goods, quantum & advanced compute is the frontier tower, run with a pragmatist's discipline. That is the baseline pattern; the differentiator is what it connects to: quantum readiness & strategy, quantum optimization for enterprise problems, post-quantum cryptography migration — delivered on Dataq Quanta and Dataq Sentinel with the sector's regulatory posture built in.

items: Demand signals too slow
Batch demand models react to last week; promotions, weather and local events shift baskets daily. Markdown decisions and replenishment both inherit the lag.
Personalization without privacy architecture
Personalization programs stall between marketing ambition and privacy office veto; consent, preference and profiling rules are retrofitted after launch.
Replenishment and allocation by rules of thumb
Store allocation, DC replenishment and size-curve decisions run on legacy heuristics; phantom availability and overstock coexist across the network.

blocks.x: Two regimes anchor the control design here: EUDR (where applicable) and Price-transparency/consumer-protection rules. Dynamic pricing constraints by jurisdiction. Evidence for both is generated by the delivery itself — control tests, replay trails and documentation are artifacts of the program, not a reconstruction project.

The rhythm is fixed on purpose: progress becomes visible from week one, not after the first steering meeting. Weeks 1–2 lock the baseline with your team: the current metric is measured, signed and stored as the reference for every later gate. Weeks 3–8 run the pilot on deliberately narrow scope — one decision path, one workflow, one plant or one portfolio — with a control owner named on your side. Weeks 9–12 industrialize what worked: runbooks, monitoring, enablement and a measured delta against the signed baseline. Anything that misses its gate is stopped or redirected with a documented decision, never quietly extended.
